entries.name: Curtis Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies cancer systems biology, combining experimental, computational and AI approaches to improve cancer diagnosis, treatment and early detection. Core themes are quantifying and forecasting tumour evolutionary dynamics, and linking genotype to phenotype in malignancy. Current work includes early cancer evolution (for example Barrett's esophagus and intestinal metaplasia) and breast cancer progression, studied with multiomic profiling, organoid models and single-cell and spatial transcriptomics. A further goal is robust biomarkers that guide treatment decisions, with AI/ML methods for spatial multiomics and histology-based prediction.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with cancer genomics, somatic evolution, computational/ML methods and single-cell/spatial omics in cancer; less emphasis on structural variants or WGS pipelines specifically, and a US visa would likely be required.

entries.name: Van Loo Lab
entries.focus: The lab takes a 'molecular archeology of cancer' approach, using whole-genome sequencing and other genomic data to reconstruct how tumours evolve. It works out subclonal architecture, copy-number changes and timelines of somatic mutation. Its work includes coordinating the PCAWG evolution and heterogeneity analysis of 2,658 cancers. The lab also studies metastasis and therapy resistance, and the role of DNA methylation and epigenetics in tumour evolution. Its disease interests include pancreatic and colorectal cancer, other gastrointestinal cancers, and sarcoma. The lab is computational and develops algorithms and statistical methods for cancer genomics.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with the student's interests in tumour whole-genome sequencing, somatic mutation and structural-variant analysis, and computational methods. Single-cell and spatial omics is the weakest overlap.

entries.name: Alexandrov Lab
entries.focus: The lab uses large-scale omics datasets and machine learning to study the mutational and non-mutational processes that drive cancer initiation and progression. It is best known for mutational signature analysis and the SigProfiler tool suite, which covers single-base substitutions, indels, copy number and structural variants. Work includes APOBEC mutagenesis, clonal hematopoiesis, tumour evolution, and germline-somatic interactions. Experimental work includes duplex sequencing of normal tissues, and the lab is also developing deep learning on histopathology slides. The goals are cancer prevention, early detection and targeted treatment, and the lab is part of the Cancer Grand Challenges CAUSE project on environmental exposures.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with cancer WGS, somatic mutation and structural-variant signature analysis, and ML methods for genomics. Single-cell and spatial omics are not a main focus, and a US role would need a visa.

entries.name: Getz Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops computational methods to characterize cancer genomes. It catalogs somatic events (mutations, copy-number changes, structural variants) and the processes that cause them during clonal evolution. It compares DNA, RNA and protein changes between tumour and normal samples. It analyzes large patient cohorts to find driver genes and pathways, molecular subtypes, and links to clinical variables. The lab co-leads the TCGA Genome Data Analysis Center and the Broad Proteogenomics Data Analysis Center. Current interests include tumour heterogeneity and clonal evolution, single-cell and spatial analysis of tumours and their microenvironment, therapy resistance, proteogenomics, and somatic mutations in normal tissues.

fit.reason: This is a very close match to nearly all the student's interests: tumour WGS/RNA analysis, somatic mutation and structural variant methods, computational methods for genomics, and single-cell and spatial cancer work. The main constraint is that it is a US lab, so a visa would be needed.

entries.name: Ideker Lab
entries.focus: The lab maps the hierarchical architecture of human cells. It integrates protein, transcriptional and genetic interaction networks, and it builds interpretable deep-learning models of cell structure and function. Applications in cancer include network-based biomarkers for patient subtyping, CRISPR/Cas9 synthetic-lethal interaction mapping, and drug-response prediction. Other work covers epigenetic aging and psychiatric disease. The lab also builds software and infrastructure such as Cytoscape and NDEx, and it leads the NCI Cancer Cell Map Initiative, NIH Bridge2AI Cell Maps for AI (CM4AI) and ARPA-H ADAPT (dynamic digital tumors).

entries.name: Laboratory of Evolutionary Design
entries.department_hint: Innovation Investigator, Arc Institute; Assistant Professor of Chemical Engineering, Stanford
entries.focus: The lab works at the intersection of machine learning and biology. It builds generative models of biological sequence (proteins, genes and genomes) trained on evolutionary data. One theme is learning from nature, for example how the immune system balances short-term protection against long-term adaptability, in order to design more robust therapeutics. A second theme is accelerating evolution by learning evolutionary rules from data so that machine learning can harness evolution. A third is safe biological AI: generative models that help researchers quickly counter harmful biology.

entries.name: Segre Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops computational and statistical genetics methods to find the genetic and biological causes of common eye diseases, including age-related macular degeneration, glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy. Most polygenic disease associations fall in noncoding regions. The lab therefore integrates epigenomic data, eQTLs and transcriptomes with genome-wide association and sequencing studies, and uses them to fine-map noncoding signals and to run pathway analyses of rare and common variants. Other directions are pharmacogenomics of adverse ocular drug responses, drug repurposing and adverse-effect prediction through cross-trait genetic analyses, and links between rare and common retinal degeneration. The lab also contributes to the GTEx and single-cell atlas work, including a multi-tissue cell atlas.

entries.name: Uhler Lab
entries.department_hint: Core Institute Member; Eric and Wendy Schmidt Center
entries.focus: The lab develops machine learning methods that combine and translate between very different types of biological data. It also builds methods that infer causal or regulatory relationships from that data. A major application is single-cell perturbation data, such as drug, knockout and overexpression screens, where the lab predicts the effects of unseen perturbations. A particular interest is how genome packing (chromatin organization) relates to gene regulation in health and disease. The lab's postdocs are co-advised with imaging, spatial and single-cell groups (Fei Chen, Xiao Wang, Paul Blainey, Ramnik Xavier, Eliezer Van Allen), so the lab touches spatial omics and some cancer-related work.

fit.reason: The lab overlaps on computational and ML methods for genomics and on single-cell and spatial omics, with some cancer co-advising (Van Allen). It does not focus on tumour WGS, structural variants or somatic mutation analysis, and the student would likely need a US visa.

entries.name: Patel Lab
entries.focus: The group develops computational and AI methods to analyze how genetics and environment jointly shape health and disease. Core work is exposome research, including leading the NEXUS network (Network for Exposomics in the United States). They integrate multi-omics data (proteomic, regulomic, exposomic and microbiome) with real-world data such as EHRs, claims, wearables and satellite data. They also use machine learning to predict individual health trajectories (for example lung function, diabetes and brain aging). A meta-science strand studies the robustness of big-data findings, using the 'vibration of effects' approach.

fit.reason: The lab shares an interest in computational and machine learning methods, but it works on population-scale exposomics and epidemiology, not tumour sequencing, structural variants, or single-cell/spatial cancer omics. It also would need a US visa.

entries.name: Smillie Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies host-microbiome interactions in the human gut, using cell atlases of the colon and enteric nervous system and spatial transcriptomics. It predicts multicellular circuits that link microbes and metabolites to tissue physiology and disease, especially inflammatory bowel disease. A third theme is computational method development for spatial transcriptomics, covering cell-cell interaction inference and linking disease-risk genetics to cells and pathways.

entries.focus: The lab uses machine learning to interpret genetic variation and to design biological molecules. It has three areas: (1) learning the 'language of life', which uses evolutionary couplings between co-mutating amino acids to study protein and RNA structure and function; (2) predicting the effects of single and combined mutations and designing stable, functional protein sequences; and (3) viral evolution and immunology, which predicts viral escape and pathogenicity, improves immune recognition and identifies antibody targets. Current members also work on T-cell receptor and antibody models, immune repertoires, enzyme and protein dynamics, and interpretable ML for single-cell and spatial transcriptomics. The lab's tagline is 'Machine learning to accelerate biology'.

entries.name: Robinson Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies genetic influences on behaviour and cognition, with an emphasis on neurodevelopmental variation and on differences within and between neuropsychiatric disorders. entries.name: Rheinbay Lab
entries.focus: The lab identifies and functionally characterizes non-coding driver mutations in tumour whole-genome sequences. It does this mainly by developing new computational analysis methods and collaborating with experimental groups. A second theme is breast and prostate cancer genomics and epigenomics, including the FOXA1 oncogene and its regulatory-element and 3' UTR mutations. A third theme is the role of the sex chromosomes in cancer, especially loss of the Y chromosome (LOY). The lab is building specialized tools to define Y chromosome status in tumours, which is hard because the chromosome is repetitive. The PI co-led the PCAWG non-coding driver analysis of 2,658 whole genomes (Nature, 2020).

fit.reason: The lab's work on tumour whole-genome somatic mutation analysis and computational method development matches the student's core interests, but I saw no evidence of single-cell/spatial or transcriptome-focused work, and a US role would likely need a visa.

entries.name: Macosko Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops genomics technologies to study brain diseases, especially schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease. It builds high-throughput single-cell and spatial methods, including Drop-seq, Slide-seq and Slide-tags. The lab applies them to identify new brain cell types, cellular responses to psychological stress, and neurons that are vulnerable to neurodegeneration.

entries.name: Getz Lab (Cancer Genome Computational Analysis)
entries.focus: The lab develops and applies computational methods to characterize and interpret cancer genomes. Characterization covers cataloguing genomic events and their mechanisms across tumour evolution, and comparing DNA, RNA and protein data between tumour and normal samples. Interpretation covers analysis across patient cohorts to find driver genes and pathways, molecular subtypes, and links to clinical variables. Current interests listed on the Broad profile are tumour heterogeneity and clonal evolution, single-cell analysis of tumours and their microenvironment, drivers of therapy resistance, proteogenomics, and somatic mutations in normal tissues. The group also builds analysis software and pipelines, and it has co-led TCGA Genome Data Analysis Center efforts.

Methods include live-cell time-lapse microscopy, quantitative single-cell imaging and mathematical modelling. A recent NIH grant summary describes extending this work to p53 dynamics across cancer models, species and tissues in vivo. The lab website lists no per-person research descriptions.

The group describes itself as combining statistical genetics with experimental genomics, for example massively parallel reporter assays.

entries.focus: The lab develops computational methods for single-cell, spatial and temporal genomics data, mainly applied to inflammatory disease. Other areas are spatial mapping of gene and protein expression to reconstruct pathological tissue structures in inflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases, and temporal mapping to predict what drives pathogenic cell states. It releases its tools as open-source software on GitHub.

entries.name: Kellis Lab
entries.focus: The lab aims to explain the mechanistic basis of human disease by combining computational and experimental methods. It systematically finds functional elements in the human genome, maps the gene-regulatory circuits that control them, and validates those circuits. Methods include epigenomic annotation of regulatory regions across cell types, comparative genomics, and single-cell and single-nucleus profiling. Disease areas include brain disorders (Alzheimer's, schizophrenia, PTSD), metabolism (obesity, diabetes, exercise), and cancer genomics. Recent work includes multi-tissue H3K27ac profiling of GTEx samples, the effect of APOE4 on myelination, and host-response remodeling by SARS-CoV-2 variants.

entries.name: Daly Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops statistical and computational methods to find and interpret genetic variation in complex human disease. Major areas are neuropsychiatric genetics (autism, schizophrenia, ADHD, eating disorders) and gene mapping in inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis). It is not cancer or somatic genomics.

entries.name: Bulyk Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies transcriptional regulation, in particular cis-regulatory elements and how sequence-specific transcription factors (TFs) recognise their DNA binding sites. It develops high-throughput experimental technologies, including protein binding microarrays and related in vitro binding assays, to measure the DNA-binding specificities of TFs and of synthetically designed proteins. The lab pairs these assays with computational and genomic analysis, with applications in human and fly, including the effects of non-coding variants on regulatory function.

entries.name: Meyerson Lab
entries.focus: The lab uses genomic approaches to find the causes of human cancers and turn those findings into therapies. It uses whole-genome sequencing to study DNA changes inside and outside the coding genome, including enhancer rearrangements that change gene expression, and long-read sequencing of structural variants. Lung cancer work covers kinase signaling, splicing-factor mutations (such as U2AF1), inflammatory signaling and aneuploidy. The lab also finds microbes linked to cancer, such as Fusobacterium in colorectal cancer, and works on genome-inspired drug discovery, which led to the EGFR/HER2 inhibitor sevabertinib.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with tumour whole-genome sequencing, structural variants and somatic mutation analysis (including regulatory-element copy-number and long-read SV projects), but there is little single-cell/spatial or ML-methods work, and the lab has wet-lab and US visa considerations.

entries.focus: The lab studies how genomic variation, especially structural variation (SV), contributes to neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism. entries.focus: The lab uses human genetics to improve diagnosis and treatment of diabetes and metabolic disease. It also leads MGH recruitment for the RADIANT study of rare and atypical diabetes, using sequencing to find new genes and variants. Methods are statistical genetics, GWAS and polygenic scores, multi-omics, and pharmacogenomics, alongside a clinical Diabetes Genetics Clinic.

entries.name: Gehlenborg Lab
entries.focus: The HIDIVE Lab studies where human and artificial intelligence meet. It builds methods and tools that help people and machines work with biomedical data and draw insights from it. The lab combines biomedical informatics, data visualization, and AI/ML. Its tools are mainly interactive visualization and exploration software, including genome-mapped views such as HiGlass-style genome interaction map viewers. The data types it works with include cancer genomics, epigenomics and nucleome data, spatial and single-cell tissue atlases (HuBMAP), and clinical data. It also runs human-factors work such as eye-tracking studies of how people read visualizations. This is a visualization and tool-building lab, not a sequencing or variant-calling lab.

entries.name: Rigollet Lab
entries.focus: The group works at the interface of statistics, machine learning and optimization, with a focus on high-dimensional statistical methods. One theme models transformers as interacting particle systems, where self-attention acts as a velocity field that moves tokens, and studies the resulting clustering behaviour. A second theme applies Wasserstein gradient flows and optimal transport to statistics and ML, including particle-based variational inference and nonparametric maximum likelihood. A third theme applies transformers and probability-measure methods to biological data, treating cell populations as probability measures, for example to predict treatment response in patient-derived organoids. The group does this work with the Schmidt Center at the Broad Institute and is recruiting postdocs on maths-biology and genomics.

entries.name: Beroukhim Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops computational approaches to interpret cancer genomes. This includes detecting copy-number alterations and rearrangements (structural variants) across many cancer types. It integrates genetic and functional genomic data to find therapeutic vulnerabilities linked to copy-number changes. A 2023 Nature paper, with the Taylor lab, applied a new aneuploidy and selection algorithm to more than 10,000 cancers.

entries.name: Duan Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops statistical and machine-learning methods for disease risk prediction using electronic health records (EHR) and EHR-linked biobanks. It also works on detecting cross-phenotype associations and pleiotropy in high-dimensional data. Another strand is federated learning and meta-analysis, which lets researchers integrate data across sites without sharing individual-level data. A fourth strand is methods for imperfect real-world data, including missing data and measurement error. The work is mostly statistical methodology rather than cancer-specific or sequencing-focused.

It has no visible work on cancer genomics, tumour WGS or transcriptomes, structural variants, or single-cell and spatial omics.

entries.name: Hormoz Lab
entries.focus: The lab is a quantitative systems biology group that asks how a cell's biological history shapes its future fate. Experimentalists, theorists and computational scientists work together on this. Experimental work includes engineering cells to record lineage and signaling histories in their own DNA, in situ barcoding with transcriptome readout, and long-term time-lapse imaging in mammalian mother machines. Model systems include human gastruloids and organoids of early embryonic development, and blood stem and progenitor cells derived from embryonic stem cells. Computational work includes differentiable models of development, and population genetics and stochastic-process models that reconstruct the origins of blood cancers. The lab also does directed viral evolution for gene delivery and single-cell RNA-seq of bacteria.

fit.reason: There is modest overlap through single-cell omics and one student's blood-cancer clonal-origins modelling. The lab is mostly developmental systems biology and cell engineering. It does little tumour WGS or structural-variant work, and the roles are at a US institution that would likely need a visa.

entries.name: Naqvi Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how quantitative control of gene expression shapes development and the 'tipping points' that lead to disease. It focuses on transcription factor (TF) dosage. It uses chemical-genetic approaches to modulate TF levels in fine increments in human stem cells and their derived cell types, such as neural crest. The lab pairs these perturbations with functional genomics and builds predictive computational and machine learning models of the molecular, cellular and morphological effects. The goal is to identify the regulatory elements, genes and cell states most sensitive to dosage changes. The PI's earlier work covered cis-regulatory divergence between human and chimpanzee, and sex-biased gene expression in mammals.

fit.reason: Computational modelling and machine learning for functional genomics overlap with the student's methods interests, but the lab studies developmental gene regulation in stem cell models, not cancer genomics, tumour sequencing or structural variants, and it is in the US, so the student may need a visa

entries.name: Sunyaev Lab
entries.focus: The lab is a computational genetics group studying human genetic variation from evolutionary, functional and medical-genetics angles. Topics include the origin and mechanisms of germline mutation (mutation-rate maps, DNA repair preferences, microsatellite expansion), and negative and recessive selection on deleterious alleles. It also covers the genetics of complex and Mendelian traits. Methods are population-genetic modeling, statistical methods for large sequencing and GWAS datasets, and machine-learning variant-effect predictors such as PolyPhen-2 and DeMAG. Cancer-related work exists but is a minor part of the group, for example ML for tumour progression in a student co-advised with the Van Allen lab.

The work is mostly autoimmune and immune-disease genetics, not cancer.

entries.name: McCarroll Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how human genome variation, including large deletions, duplications and rearrangements, shapes risk of disease. A major emphasis is brain disorders such as Huntington's disease, schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. Recent work shows how an expanding DNA repeat drives brain cell death in Huntington's disease. The lab developed single-cell methods such as Drop-Seq and uses single-cell and single-nucleus gene expression to study cell types and somatic variation. It has also done earlier work on C4 complement genes in schizophrenia and on clonal hematopoiesis, a pre-cancerous blood condition.

entries.name: Ge Lab
entries.focus: The Ge Lab works on statistical genetics, psychiatric genetics and neuroimaging genetics. It builds statistical, computational and machine-learning methods for large genomic, neuroimaging, behavioural and electronic health record datasets. Its stated goals are to characterise the genetic architecture of complex traits, uncover the genetic and neural basis of brain structure and mental disorders, and improve individualised prediction of disease risk, onset and progression. Recent outputs include SuSiEx cross-ancestry fine-mapping, real-time dynamic polygenic prediction, multi-ancestry polygenic scores, individualised cortical parcellation from fMRI, and copy number variation in schizophrenia. Current NIH R01 funding covers multi-ancestry genetic methods and the genetics of ADHD.

fit.reason: Methods-heavy statistical and machine-learning genomics overlaps a little with the student's computational interests, but the lab does germline and population genetics of psychiatric and brain traits, not cancer, tumour sequencing, structural variants or single-cell and spatial omics.

entries.name: Wold Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies transcriptional regulatory networks in mouse and human. It is a long-standing ENCODE consortium group and holds an active NIH award (UM1HG009443) for higher-precision human and mouse transcriptomes, including aging and Alzheimer's-related tissue comparisons. Its recent work builds long-read RNA-seq (PacBio) methods and the ENCODE4 long-read collection, which has hundreds of libraries across human and mouse samples. It also pairs long-read sequencing with single-cell and spatial transcriptomics to resolve isoform expression, and has produced a bulk and single-cell atlas of postnatal regulatory events across mouse tissues.

fit.reason: There is some overlap in transcriptome sequencing, single-cell/spatial omics and computational genomics methods, but the lab works on normal mouse and human regulation and isoforms, not cancer genomics, structural variants or somatic mutations. A US visa would also likely be needed.

entries.focus: The lab studies how non-coding RNAs and the 3D organization of the nucleus control gene expression and cell state. The lab builds its own methods: SPRITE for multi-way DNA/RNA/protein contacts, CLAP and SPIDR for RNA-protein interactions, and ChIP-DIP for multiplexed chromatin mapping. It combines these with computational analysis, CRISPR screens and single-cell assays. It also studies RNA toxicity from the C9ORF72 repeat expansion in ALS.

entries.name: Aryee Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops computational and statistical methods to extract signal from noisy genomic datasets, with an emphasis on cancer epigenomics. Its stated themes are tissue architecture, nuclear organization and regulatory DNA loops. For tissue architecture, it analyses spatially resolved data such as spatial transcriptomics and chromatin imaging to see how cell neighbourhoods shape cell state in solid tumours. For nuclear organization, it uses imaging and 3D genome mapping to link nuclear morphology seen in cancer diagnosis to gene activity and disease progression. For regulatory loops, it builds tools to identify and statistically test dynamic, transient chromatin loops that connect distant regulatory elements to promoters.

fit.reason: The lab's computational methods and its spatial omics in solid tumours match two of the student's interests, but it focuses on epigenomics and 3D genome rather than whole-genome sequencing, structural variants or somatic mutation analysis, and a US role may need a visa.

entries.focus: The group uses computational methods to study how macromolecules change shape and how those conformational changes contribute to common human diseases. Its biophysics work includes modeling the unfolded states of intrinsically disordered proteins (tau, alpha-synuclein, amyloid beta), collagen structure and collagenolysis, and fibronectin unfolding with steered molecular dynamics. Current students also work on robustness and fairness of clinical ML and on multimodal and single-cell biological data.

entries.name: Alm Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies the human microbiome's role in health and disease. It combines computational and experimental methods, with the aim of engineering the microbiome and moving discoveries quickly into clinical care. Current work includes microbial community therapeutics, synthetic microbial communities and culturing, and microbial ecology and evolution (for example, vaginal microbes and genome/isolate collections for GWAS). Another major theme is wastewater-based epidemiology, which includes city-level outbreak detection, COVID-19 tracking and viral metagenomics. The lab is also developing smart sewers, smart toilets and low-cost noninvasive biomarkers.

fit.reason: The lab has strong computational and metagenomics strengths, but it works on microbiome and wastewater epidemiology, not cancer genomics, structural variants, somatic mutation analysis, or single-cell/spatial cancer omics.

entries.name: Mirny Lab
entries.focus: The lab uses polymer physics, simulation and statistical mechanics together with genomic data analysis to study how chromosomes are folded and how that folding works in the cell. A central topic is loop extrusion by SMC complexes (cohesin and condensin). The lab studies how extrusion shapes 3D genome organization, enhancer-promoter communication and sister-chromatid organization, using Hi-C data analysis and Bayesian inference. Related work covers epigenetic memory through mitosis and cell fate, nuclear organization and mechanics, and DNA repair and gene activation dynamics studied by single-particle tracking. The lab also develops computational tools and some machine-learning methods. The PI's earlier work includes cancer evolution and somatic mutations, and an alumnus (Carino Gurjao) worked in that area, but cancer genomics is not the current focus of the listed members.

fit.reason: The lab's computational genomics and Hi-C methods overlap loosely with the student's interests, but its current work is chromatin biophysics, with little on cancer genomics, structural variants, tumour sequencing or single-cell/spatial cancer omics, and US roles would need a visa.

entries.name: Bathe Lab
entries.focus: The lab treats DNA and RNA as programmable construction materials and designs nanoscale structures with controlled shape, composition and function. Biomedical work includes DNA-based virus-like particles for vaccines and active immunotherapies, and structured nucleic-acid nanoparticles for delivering genetic medicines to specific cells and tissues, including the brain. Other projects arrange quantum dots and chromophores on DNA scaffolds for quantum photonics and sensing. Further topics are DNA data storage and computing, ambient-temperature preservation of genomic information, multiplexed neuronal profiling and engineered functional RNA assemblies. Methods are mainly wet-lab nanotechnology and biophysics, with computational design and modelling of the nucleic-acid structures.

fit.reason: The lab works on DNA/RNA nanomaterials, delivery and photonics, so it has almost no overlap with cancer genomics, structural variants, sequencing analysis or single-cell/spatial omics. The only loose link is computational design and DNA-based neuronal barcoding and profiling.

entries.focus: The lab builds computational and experimental tools to study how tumors evolve at the genetic, epigenetic, metabolic and microenvironmental levels. One main area is how copy-number alterations, especially extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA), change across space and time in cancer cell populations. A second area is new methods for tracing cell lineages, including the Cassiopeia phylogenetic inference tools and the PEtracer spatial lineage-tracing approach. One goal is to remove experimental bottlenecks and raise the throughput and quality of data collection. A second goal is to measure and explain how biomolecules, cells and organisms behave over short timescales and in response to perturbations. The lab also builds methods with collaborators for unmet research and medical needs and shares its technologies. Their work is mostly assay and instrument development, such as single-cell and high-throughput microfluidic and imaging platforms, rather than cancer-specific genomics. entries.focus: The lab studies how individual bacterial species and strains behave in the human microbiome, with the aim of enabling microbial therapies. entries.name: Cardona Group (connectomics)
entries.focus: The group does experimental and comparative connectomics. It maps synaptic wiring diagrams of small brains, mainly the larval fruit fly (Drosophila), and also other small animals across the animal phylogenetic tree, using volume electron microscopy. The work has moved from sensory and motor circuits to deeper regions such as the mushroom body (memory) and the central complex (spatial learning and motor planning). Methods combine EM reconstruction, behavioural analysis, electrophysiology and optophysiology, open-source image-analysis software, and computational circuit models that link connectivity to behaviour. Recent computational work includes analyses of synaptic density and wiring optimisation across species.

fit.reason: The lab works on neural circuit connectomics and EM image analysis, with no cancer genomics, sequencing, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics. The only overlap is generic computational and ML methods.

entries.name: Landau Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies somatic evolution: how single cells accumulate mutations over a lifetime and how the resulting clonal expansions affect health and cancer. It uses genotype-aware single-cell multiomics on human samples. This compares mutant and wild-type cells from the same patient to find mutation-specific phenotypes. It also does whole-genome sequencing of cell-free plasma DNA for liquid biopsy, aiming to detect circulating tumour DNA at parts-per-million fractions without a matched tumour sample. A third line of work is human single-cell lineage tracing, which builds somatic phylogenies from intrinsic genetic barcodes together with phenotyping. The lab combines computational and experimental tools to study cancer evolution and to design precision-medicine approaches that overcome it.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with single-cell cancer omics, computational methods and WGS-based cfDNA and somatic mutation analysis; it is less centred on structural variants or tumour transcriptome profiling, and a US visa would be needed.

entries.focus: The lab develops machine-learning methods, especially chemical language models, to illuminate the 'dark matter' of mass spectrometry-based metabolomics. An NIH DP5 grant describes two further tools: DecipherMS, which annotates unknown structures from MS/MS spectra, and FoundationMS, a foundation model for metabolomics. Earlier work covers generative chemical language models, including the finding that invalid SMILES outputs can improve model performance, and computational proteomics.

It is best known for AutoDock and AutoDock Vina, the widely used ligand-protein docking programs. Other work includes mesoscale models of cellular environments (cellPACK, cellPAINT), the Python Molecular Viewer, and 3D printing and augmented reality for research and education. Applied work focuses on structure-based design of anti-HIV inhibitors and chemical probes, including covalent inhibitors and drug resistance.

entries.name: Forli Lab
entries.focus: The lab builds computational tools for structure-based drug discovery and uses them on therapeutic targets. A central effort is the AutoDock suite, including GPU-accelerated docking engines, improved force fields and scoring functions, and search algorithms. Many projects are joint with experimental labs and cover membrane proteins, ion channels, neurodegeneration and the unfolded protein response.

entries.name: Kundaje Lab
entries.focus: The lab builds machine learning and deep learning models that predict gene regulation from DNA and RNA sequence. It uses these models to interpret the sequence rules (motifs and syntax) that control gene activity. It applies them to non-coding genetic variants in disease, including colorectal cancer, cardiometabolic, neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric conditions. entries.name: Sidow Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies the evolution of function, which it currently applies to cancer. entries.name: Engelhardt Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops statistical and machine-learning models to find the biological mechanisms behind complex traits and disease. entries.name: Lundberg Lab
entries.focus: The lab works on spatial proteomics and cell biology, combining bioimaging, proteomics and AI to map where human proteins sit in cells at subcellular resolution. It asks how protein localisation varies across space, time and single cells, and how mislocalisation contributes to disease. It contributes to the Subcellular Atlas of the Human Protein Atlas and aims to build a spatiotemporal proteome model of the human cell, including 'virtual cell' and digital-twin models. Methods include immunofluorescence and multiplexed imaging, mass spectrometry, Deep Visual Proteomics, and deep learning, foundation and generative models on microscopy data. The lab also runs crowd-sourced and citizen-science challenges.

entries.name: Rusu Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops analytic methods for integrating biomedical data, especially radiology-pathology fusion and MRI-ultrasound fusion for guiding procedures. Pathology labels are mapped onto radiology images so that deep learning models can detect cancer and separate aggressive from indolent disease at the pixel level. Most of the work is on prostate cancer MRI, in close collaboration with the Urologic Cancer Innovation Lab. The lab also works on breast and kidney cancer, and on some non-oncologic applications. Methods include image registration, computer vision, multimodal machine learning and self-supervised learning.

fit.reason: It is a computational cancer lab, so it overlaps on machine learning for cancer. Its data are radiology and pathology images, not sequencing, structural variants, or single-cell and spatial omics, so it overlaps little with the student's genomics focus.

entries.name: Plevritis Lab
entries.focus: The lab does computational modeling of cancer biology and cancer outcomes. It builds stochastic models of the natural history of cancer from clinical research data. It uses these models to estimate population-level outcomes under different screening and treatment strategies. It also analyzes genomic and proteomic data, including single-cell and spatial data, to find molecular networks disrupted in cancer initiation and progression and to link them to patient outcomes. The lab's affiliated projects are CCSB, IIBIS and CSBS. Plevritis also serves as Associate Director for Cancer AI at the Stanford Cancer Institute.

fit.reason: The lab's single-cell/spatial cancer omics and ML/statistical methods overlap with the student's interests, but it has little focus on whole-genome sequencing, structural variants or somatic mutation analysis, and the student would need a US visa.

entries.name: Hernandez-Boussard Lab
entries.focus: The lab uses data science to improve healthcare quality, outcomes, equity and health policy. It works at the intersection of informatics and population health, and promotes responsible AI across populations. Its methods are applied to large clinical datasets such as administrative claims and electronic health records, for comparative effectiveness research and evaluation of healthcare quality. The lab's work centres on clinical prediction models and fairness/bias evaluation of AI. It also covers accountability measures and health policy. Some work in the lab involves postoperative outcomes and opioid use, using the OMOP common data model. I found no evidence of a cancer genomics or sequencing focus.

fit.reason: The lab works on EHR/claims-based clinical AI, health equity and health policy, with no apparent work on cancer genomics, tumour sequencing, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics; the only overlap is general machine-learning methodology.

entries.name: Greenleaf Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops high-throughput genomic and biophysical methods. Its research areas are listed as High-throughput Biophysics & Evolution and Accessible DNA & Chromatin Structure. Chromatin work builds on assays such as ATAC-seq and single-cell and multiomic profiling of the epigenome, applied to gene regulation and to disease, including cancer. The biophysics work uses massively parallel platforms to measure molecular interactions of nucleic acids and proteins. The lab also works on RNA medicine (the RAMP program). The research description above comes from the page's section titles and link names, and I did not read those research pages themselves, so it is not a full description.

fit.reason: Single-cell and multiomic chromatin methods plus computational work overlap with the student's single-cell omics and ML interests, but the lab is not focused on tumour WGS, structural variants or somatic mutation analysis, and a US role would probably need a visa.

entries.name: Qiu Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies the gene regulatory networks and cell-cell interactions that drive mammalian cell-fate transitions over time and space. Its emphasis is heart evolution, development and disease. It combines machine learning (transformers, neural ODEs, diffusion models) with systems-biology models. Experiments include scRNA-seq, spatial transcriptomics, metabolic labeling and Perturb-seq, and the aim is to predict cell states under perturbation. The lab builds open-source tools such as Monocle, Dynamo, Spateo, PantheonOS and Bio-Babel.

fit.reason: It overlaps on computational/ML methods and single-cell/spatial omics, but the lab works on developmental and cardiac biology, not cancer genomics, tumour WGS, or structural/somatic variants. The student would also need a US visa.

entries.name: Integrative Cancer Epidemiology Group
entries.focus: The group studies the causes and prevention of cancer, with a strong emphasis on breast cancer. It integrates epidemiologic, genetic and tissue-based biomarker data from large population cohorts, notably the Generations Study. Work includes polygenic and multifactorial risk prediction models, lifestyle and hormonal risk factors, and studies of benign breast biopsies as markers of future cancer. These are population-scale statistical and epidemiological methods, not tumour sequencing. They are being extended with AI and data-science projects.

fit.reason: Their genetic and risk-modelling work touches computational methods for genomics. They do population epidemiology rather than tumour WGS, structural variants, or single-cell and spatial omics, and a UK role would likely need a visa.

entries.name: Andrés Group (population/evolutionary genomics), UCL Genetics Institute
entries.focus: The group studies how organisms adapt to their natural environments and how natural selection shapes genomic diversity within and between populations. It has worked mainly on humans and other primates, and now also on Drosophila. Methods are population genetics, bioinformatics and genomics, including ancestral recombination graph inference and analysis of modern and ancient genomes, plus functional approaches.

entries.name: Curtis group (statistical genetics)
entries.focus: Curtis develops statistical methods for rare-variant association analysis of exome and genome sequence data. His main approach is a weighted burden test, where each variant is weighted by rarity and predicted functional effect and the weights are summed into a gene-wise score per person. This is implemented in his own programs, such as GENEVARASSOC and SCOREASSOC, which are combined with logistic and linear regression. He applies these methods to about 200,000 exome-sequenced UK Biobank participants for traits such as type 2 diabetes, BMI, hyperlipidaemia and psychiatric referral. He also builds exome-wide risk scores for schizophrenia. The work concerns germline complex-trait and psychiatric genetics, not cancer.

fit.reason: The work is germline rare-variant statistics for psychiatric and complex traits in UK Biobank, with no cancer, tumour sequencing, structural variants or single-cell/spatial work, and the group appears to be essentially a solo PI.

entries.name: Hellenthal Group (statistical genetics, human population history)
entries.department_hint: Genetics, Evolution and Environment / UCL Genetics Institute
entries.focus: The group develops statistical and Bayesian methods for genetic data, with an emphasis on human population structure and demographic history. Its best-known methods are the admixture-inference tools GLOBETROTTER and fastGLOBETROTTER, which date and characterise historical mixing between populations, and the group maintains these on GitHub. Applications include population structure and movements in Africa (including Ethiopia), the genetic structure of the UK, and the effect of Anglo-Saxon migration on adaptive variants and health in the UK. Current work also covers detecting loci under adaptation to new environments and statistical models for loci with methylation marks set in the early embryo. The work draws on ancient DNA and worldwide genotype/haplotype data. It does not involve cancer genomics.

entries.name: Comparative Somatic Evolutionary Genomics
entries.focus: The group studies how somatic mutations and clonal expansions accumulate in normal tissues as animals age, and what this means for health. They use laser capture microdissection with low-input genome sequencing to measure somatic mutation burden and mutational signatures across many species. The work has three strands. Ageing: comparing mutation rates and clonal dynamics in species with different lifespans. Cancer: looking at long-lived, large-bodied species such as whales for cancer-resistance mechanisms. Environmental monitoring: using mutational signatures in sentinel species to track the effects of pollutants. A Wellcome grant covers a comparative study of somatic evolution across about 30 species.

fit.reason: The lab overlaps with the student's interest in somatic mutation analysis and computational genomics, but it works on normal tissue across species rather than on tumour WGS/transcriptome, structural variants or single-cell/spatial cancer omics, and a UK role may need a visa.

Work is largely mathematical modelling and biophysical theory tied to experimental clonal and single-cell data, rather than tumour sequencing.

entries.focus: The group is a small one working on human and pathogen genomics, mainly Plasmodium falciparum malaria. entries.name: Meier Group
entries.focus: The group studies speciation and evolutionary genomics. It asks why some lineages speciate far faster than others, and how hybridisation and chromosomal rearrangements (fusions, fissions, translocations, inversions) contribute to rapid speciation and adaptation. It sequences and compares genomes of Ithomiini and Heliconius butterflies, peacock spiders and other insects, and combines these with behavioural and ecological fieldwork. Methods include population genomics, comparative analysis of chromosome-level genomes (Project Psyche, Darwin Tree of Life), structural-variant and breakpoint analysis, and single-cell sperm sequencing. The PI's earlier work on Lake Victoria cichlids showed that hybridisation fuelled adaptive radiations.

fit.reason: Methodological overlap exists in structural-variant analysis, large-scale genome comparison and some single-cell sequencing, but the work is evolutionary genomics in non-model insects, with no cancer, tumour or somatic-mutation focus.

entries.name: Taipale Group
entries.focus: The group studies how DNA sequence determines when and where genes are expressed, which it calls the 'Sequence to Expression' problem or the 'second genetic code' of transcription regulation. It measures transcription factor–DNA binding with high-throughput biochemical methods (HT-SELEX, ATI) to build biophysical models of gene expression. It tests synthetic sequences in cells with massively parallel reporter assays and uses genome editing. It trains machine-learning models to map sequence to expression, then applies them to large datasets such as cancer genomes and GWAS to interpret non-coding variants and growth control in development and cancer.

entries.focus: The group studies somatic mutations, DNA methylation and clonal dynamics in human tissues to understand how clonal selection drives ageing and cancer. The group also builds personalised cancer outcome models for clinicians, such as the NHS blood cancer prediction tool, and publishes computational tools on GitHub (nangalialab).

entries.name: Blaxter Group
entries.focus: The group studies how genomic novelty evolves and how opportunity and constraint shape present-day diversity. It produces high-quality reference genome assemblies, mainly for animals but also for plants, fungi, protists and their bacterial symbionts, within the Tree of Life Programme. Research topics include gene and species phylogenies, horizontal gene transfer versus introgression, eukaryote–bacteria and parasite–host symbioses, and the evolution of chromosome structure. It also studies meiofauna (tardigrades, nematodes and other Ecdysozoa) and the genomics of extremophilia. The group develops software for genome assembly, validation and analysis.

fit.reason: The group does computational genomics and genome-structure work, which touches the student's interest in methods and structural variation, but it has no cancer, tumour sequencing, somatic mutation or single-cell/spatial omics focus, and it is UK-based.

entries.name: Stratton Group
entries.focus: The group uses DNA sequencing to study the genome changes that accumulate over a lifetime, mainly to find the causes of cancer. Current student and postdoc projects include colibactin and gut-microbe mutagenesis in colorectal cancer, germline and early somatic mutagenesis, and mutation rates across tissues during ageing.

entries.name: Vento-Tormo Group
entries.focus: The group studies the principles of tissue organisation. It combines single-cell and spatial genomics, AI/machine learning and gene editing to build reference maps of how DNA and environmental changes reshape the cellular circuits behind disease. It also released UMA (Universal Model for Atoms), a family of universal interatomic potentials trained on the team's datasets from the past five years. The work covers chemistry, catalysis and materials, including biomolecular and electrolyte systems in OMol25. It is atomistic simulation, not genomics. I found no FAIR team doing omics, cancer genomics or single-cell work.

fit.reason: The team does atomistic chemistry and materials ML, with no genomics, cancer, structural-variant or single-cell/spatial omics work; only general ML-methods skills transfer.

entries.name: Amazon / AWS
entries.focus: AWS's healthcare and life-sciences AI group builds cloud products for pharma, biotech and academic research. In April 2026 it launched Amazon Bio Discovery, an agentic AI application for antibody drug design. It has a catalog of biological foundation models and an AI agent that helps choose models and plan experiments. Users can train models on their own experimental data without custom code. Top candidates go to partner labs (Twist Bioscience and Ginkgo Bioworks) for synthesis and testing, and the results feed back into the next design round. Early users reported include Memorial Sloan Kettering, Bayer, Voyager Therapeutics, the Broad Institute and Fred Hutch. The focus is therapeutic protein and antibody design, not genomics analysis or sequencing-based cancer research, and I found no team publishing in that area.

fit.reason: The team's public work is antibody and drug design with foundation models, which has little overlap with cancer genomics, structural variants or single-cell and spatial omics. The only overlap is general ML for biology, and MSK is a cancer-centre user of the platform.

entries.name: Illumina
entries.focus: Illumina's AI lab builds deep-learning models that predict the effect of genetic variants. SpliceAI predicts splice-altering variants, PrimateAI-3D scores missense variants, and PromoterAI scores noncoding promoter variants. SpliceAI2 (October 2026) was trained on a dataset more than 100 times larger than the original, and Illumina reports it found 17% more disease-relevant variants on a rare-disease dataset. These tools aim to resolve variants of unknown significance in rare disease and to support drug target discovery. They are delivered through Illumina Connected Software and the Emedgene interpretation platform. The BioInsight business adds large multi-omic data assets and AI software for drug discovery.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with computational and ML methods for genomics and with variant and splicing analysis, but the team's focus is germline and rare-disease variant interpretation rather than cancer, somatic SVs or single-cell and spatial work, and US/UK roles would need work authorization.

entries.name: Recursion
entries.focus: Recursion runs an automated 'lab-in-the-loop' drug discovery platform. It generates very large cell-imaging (phenomics), transcriptomic and other perturbation datasets, and uses ML to map how genetic and chemical perturbations change cell state. Valence Labs, its AI research arm (formed in 2023 with the Valence Discovery acquisition, with sites in Montreal and London), works on three themes. 'Predict' models cell responses to perturbation, including multimodal and multi-omic foundation models. 'Explain' builds causal explanations of how molecular interventions affect cell function. 'Discover' uses lab-in-the-loop engines to generate and test therapeutic hypotheses. The company's clinical pipeline is largely oncology and rare disease, and it also publishes open models and datasets.

fit.reason: Single-cell ML and computational methods for genomics overlap with the student's interests, but Recursion focuses on perturbation phenomics and drug discovery rather than tumour WGS, structural variants or somatic mutation analysis. Student programs are currently paused or have no openings.

programs.name: Open Apply (general application)
programs.requirements: The posting lists no degree, experience or skill requirements. It asks for a resume and cover letter, contact details, country and city. Two required questions cover where you would have the most impact and which locations you would work from or relocate to. LinkedIn and portfolio are optional. Applicants must be available for 1-2 weekly meetings starting at 8am PT or ending at 7pm CET, and must be able to travel several times a year for retreats and events. The company is looking for scientists, deep learning researchers, engineers and entrepreneurs.
programs.eligibility: Global applications are accepted from any location. The company prefers people who can regularly work in person at an office. The posting says nothing about students or visas. US, German or Swiss work authorization would likely be needed for an on-site role. This is a general full-time application, not a student program. The posting says some benefits do not apply to internships, but it describes no internship.
programs.location: Palo Alto, Berlin or Zurich (applying from elsewhere is allowed)
programs.deadline_text: Rolling. No closing date; the form was still live when I checked on 2026-11-08.
